analysis.one_liner: Requires Congress to affirmatively approve every major federal regulation before it can take effect.
analysis.headline: Introduced with zero cosponsors on June 6, 2000, referred to the Senate Governmental Affairs Committee, and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under this bill, any federal rule estimated to cost the economy $100 million or more — or to raise prices or hurt jobs and competition — could not take effect until both chambers of Congress passed a resolution approving it. Rules were deemed approved after a short waiting period unless 20% of members of either chamber petitioned to force an actual vote. The bill also barred courts from reviewing approved rules, permanently banned agencies from re-issuing a rule once Congress rejected it, and excluded telecommunications rules entirely.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies and industries that face costly federal regulation — on pollution, workplace safety, consumer protection, and finance — gain a powerful new chokepoint: any major rule they oppose could be blocked by getting a fifth of one chamber to sign a petition and voting it down, and the agency could not reissue it for six months.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Regulated industries facing major federal rules

how_it_helps.text: Major rules — those with $100 million or more in annual economic effect, major cost or price increases, or significant effects on competition, employment, or investment — could not take effect until Congress passed a joint resolution approving them [S2][S3].

The bill gives Congress a default 'deemed passed' clock, but if 20% of the members of either chamber file a petition within 30 days, the rule must win an actual recorded vote; a single chamber voting no kills the rule, and the agency cannot reissue it in substantially the same form for six months [S3].

Rules approved by a joint resolution (other than those deemed passed without a vote) would be shielded from judicial review, and the President could unilaterally let emergency, law-enforcement, national-security, and trade-agreement rules take effect temporarily [S3].

The bill also directs the President to establish by executive order a review program that logs and publicly discloses contacts between agency employees and outside parties, and publishes each draft of a rule as changed during White House review [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people who rely on federal protections — from clean air and water to workplace and consumer safety — bear the cost if rules they depend on stall or die in Congress, which historically struggles to pass affirmative legislation on any schedule.
analysis.who_pays_short: Everyone relying on federal safety and environmental rules

drawbacks.text: Requiring an affirmative act of Congress for every major rule would let a hostile minority — or simple congressional inaction — stall protections for clean air, worker safety, and consumer health indefinitely, since only a 20% petition is needed to remove the automatic approval [S3].
The bill excludes telecommunications rules from the definition of a major rule, carving one regulated sector out of the new process entirely [S2][S3].
Shielding approved rules from judicial review removes a check courts currently provide, and a defeated rule could not be reissued for six months even if circumstances warrant it [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The transparency provisions in Section 3 — logging outside contacts and publishing revised drafts during White House review — are genuinely useful good-government ideas. But the centerpiece, mandatory congressional approval of major rules, would convert every significant public protection into a political hostage: a well-organized fifth of either chamber could kill any rule and bar its reissuance. The cost to everyday protections outweighs the procedural benefit, and the telecom exemption undercuts its own logic.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Governmental Affairs Committee, which never acted on it, and it died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Sen. Craig Thomas (R-WY) introduced the bill on June 6, 2000, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Governmental Affairs [S1][S5].
The committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill expired with the Congress on January 3, 2001 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people who rely on federal health, safety, environmental, and consumer rules are better off, because those rules continue to take effect without needing Congress to approve each one. Regulated industries gained nothing, though they also faced no change.

for.name: Sen. Craig Thomas
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks; the bill was then referred to committee.

against.name: Senate Committee on Governmental Affairs

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill sat in committee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no senator cosponsored the bill, so the partisan split never got a chance to appear.

industries.industry: Regulated industries (manufacturing, energy, chemicals, finance and other sectors facing major federal rules)
industries.note: The bill would hand these industries a veto point over any rule costing $100 million or more: 20% of one chamber could force a vote, and one chamber voting no kills the rule and blocks reissuance for six months. That leverage would come at the expense of the health, safety, and consumer protections those rules provide.

The bill explicitly excludes rules under the Telecommunications Act of 1996 from the new approval requirement — a carve-out that leaves telecom rules under the existing process while every other major rule faces congressional approval.
